lead_title: AI agents are becoming the primary unit of enterprise compute consumption, not individual users or queries

options.conviction: L2: The infrastructure layer is still optimized for human usage patterns — but humans aren't the primary consumers anymore, agents are
options.post:
Your infrastructure assumes humans are using it.

That assumption is expensive.

Every week I see another product team optimizing for human burst patterns, thinking about peak hours, user spikes, session timeouts designed around coffee breaks.

Meanwhile 70% of Databricks queries now come from AI agents.

Not demos. Revenue-driving queries that customers pay for.

At Atlan, we've learned this firsthand building agents for GTM workflows. The agents never rest. They don't have coffee breaks. They don't work 9-to-5.

They consume compute like a river, not like rainfall.

The French startup Kog just raised funding betting that most GPU infrastructure is optimized wrong, designed for human-burst loads when agents need sustained-compute loads.

If they're right, every team building agent products needs to rethink their entire architecture stack.

- Rate limits designed for humans don't work for agents
- Pricing that assumes spiky usage misses constant consumption
- Reliability guarantees built for session patterns break on persistent workflows

Most SaaS companies are still building for yesterday's user.

IMO the teams who redesign for agent-first consumption win the next wave.

The ones still optimizing for human usage patterns get disrupted by competitors who built for the actual user.

What does your usage graph tell you about who's really using your product?

options.conviction: L3: Teams need to start measuring agent vs human consumption to understand their real usage patterns and plan infrastructure accordingly
options.post:
70% of Databricks queries now come from AI agents.

I've been watching this shift across multiple companies, but that Databricks number stopped me cold.

Not because agents are using enterprise software, that's expected.

Because 70% means agents are the majority consumer, not humans.

That's not AI adoption. That's infrastructure transformation.

Every product I see is still architected for humans:
- Session timeouts for lunch breaks
- Rate limits for typing speed
- Peak hours around work schedules

But agents don't take breaks. They don't have peak hours. They consume compute like a baseline load, not a burst pattern.

Garry Tan claims 1 person plus 20 agents beats full engineering departments at big tech companies. If true, coordination costs just collapsed.

The math is simple:
- 20 agents × continuous operation = sustained compute load
- 1 human × intermittent oversight = spiky management pattern

Your pricing model, reliability guarantees, and infrastructure planning still assume the human is doing the work.

The agent is doing the work. The human is configuring the agents.

At Atlan, when we build agents for GTM workflows, they run APIs, pull from databases, and post results where we need them. The humans never open the app while the agent is working.

That's a different usage pattern than what most SaaS products price for.

What percentage of your usage comes from agents versus humans?

If you don't know, you're planning infrastructure for yesterday's user.

options.conviction: L1: The cost of coordination is collapsing so fast that small teams with agent swarms will consistently outbuild traditional engineering teams
options.post:
Three data points from this week that connect to something bigger.

Databricks reports 70% of their queries now come from AI agents, not human analysts.

Garry Tan claims 1 person coordinating 20 AI agents outperforms full engineering departments at big tech companies.

French startup Kog raised funding to optimize GPUs for agent-sustained loads instead of human-burst patterns.

Here's what I think these connect to:

The coordination cost collapse is happening faster than anyone modeled.

Managing 20 agents requires different skills than managing 20 engineers. No performance reviews. No meetings. No interpersonal dynamics.

You configure them once and scale execution horizontally.

The bottleneck shifts from people management to prompt engineering and quality control.

Most infrastructure providers are still optimizing for human usage:
- Spiky loads during work hours
- Session-based pricing
- Rate limits designed for typing speed

But agents consume like a baseline, not a burst.

At Atlan, our agents call APIs, read databases, and integrate across systems without humans clicking buttons. They work nights, weekends, and holidays at the same intensity.

That's a different cost structure than what most teams plan for.

The teams who understand agent economics first will consistently underbid the teams who don't.

Because their cost per unit of work keeps dropping while traditional teams' costs stay flat.

How many agents is your team coordinating versus how many humans?

That ratio might predict who wins your category in 12 months.
